title: DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses
authors: Jianyuan Zhong, Chenwei Wu, Zhaochen Yu, Xixian Jiang, Xuewei Li, Hao Xiao
abstract: Scientific discovery requires developing worthwhile hypotheses into practical investigations, yet learning from this evolving research process remains challenging. We introduce an operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses: evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties, coupled with feasible investigations, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations. Our DiscoveryRSI framework develops hypothesis trees through multi-agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and recursively learns through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization attributes scientific assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay identifies productive strategies and recurring failures to refine research workflows; and rediscovery applies accepted improvements to new investigations, generating further experience for subsequent learning. We also introduce DFM-Bench, which provides comprehensive assessment of hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress at the levels of hypotheses, revisions, development paths and research runs. Across four life-science domains, automated evaluation shows that hypothesis quality rises from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self-improvement, with the large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability. We further validate hypothesis quality through expert review, comparing our DiscoveryRSI-27B with other research agents. Preliminary human assessments show that DiscoveryRSI-27B scores higher than GPT-6 Luna on hypothesis importance and whether claims are plausible and evidence-bounded. DiscoveryRSI-27B achieved a 6.3% rate of hypothesis correspondence with research published after the model cutoff, largely outperform GPT-6 with 2.5% and Claude Opus 5 with 2.3%, while delivering greater human-rated improvement along research paths.

infographic.key_insight: DiscoveryRSI recursively improves scientific hypothesis generation by learning from evidence-grounded investigations, research contributions, and workflow outcomes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework connects multi-agent hypothesis search to executable investigations, offering a design for research automation that learns across successive runs.
method: Evolve hypothesis trees with feasible tests, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations.
Compile selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks.
Attribute research credit, replay workflows, and reuse accepted improvements in new investigations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four life-science domains, automated hypothesis-quality scores rose from 4.86 to 5.39 after two improvement rounds; preliminary human review reported 6.3% correspondence with post-cutoff research versus 2.5% and 2.3% for comparison agents.
infographic.watch_item: Preliminary expert assessments and post-cutoff research correspondence do not establish prospective experimental validity or generalization beyond the evaluated domains.
infographic.paper_title: DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses

title: Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents
authors: Mingze Yin, Xiaohan Wang, Dian Li, Longfei Luo, Jiahong Yan, Yiheng Zhu
abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across complex tasks, they predominantly operate in isolated sessions, lacking the ability to continually learn from historical interactions or adapt to user-specific environments. Existing self-evolution paradigms often indiscriminately inject raw interaction trajectories into memory or skill modules, leading to obscured behavioral patterns and compromised update controllability. Furthermore, as foundational LLM reasoning improves, the bottleneck for agentic evolution shifts from accumulating generic knowledge to effectively managing situational experience. To address this, we propose Darwin-Claw, an environment-adaptive self-evolving framework that systematically distills episodic experiences to drive the comprehensive evolution of operational skills and durable memory. Theoretically grounded in an iterative agent-actor and evolver-critic co-adaptation, Darwin-Claw introduces a Hierarchical Experience Consolidation System that extracts fine-grained error attributions and generalizes them into dynamically updated prototype vectors. This structured situational experience serves as interaction patches for context-sensitive perception and explicit optimization signals for skill refinement. Practically, Darwin-Claw is a readily deployable, automated framework compatible with mainstream agent systems without requiring manual curation. Extensive experiments on WildClawBench demonstrate that Darwin-Claw yields substantial performance improvements, establishing a controllable and stable pathway for the continual, user-centric adaptation of autonomous agents in real-world ecosystems.

infographic.key_insight: Darwin-Claw turns past agent interactions into structured situational experience to support continual adaptation of skills and durable memory.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework is designed to integrate with mainstream agent systems and automate environment-specific adaptation without manual experience curation.
method: Iteratively co-adapt an agent-actor and an evolver-critic.
Attribute interaction errors and consolidate them into dynamically updated prototype vectors.
Use consolidated experience as context-sensitive interaction patches and optimization signals for skill refinement.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports substantial performance improvements on WildClawBench but provides no numerical results or experimental details.
infographic.watch_item: Long-term update stability and the risk of retaining incorrect or overly environment-specific experience require validation beyond the abstract’s claims.
infographic.paper_title: Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents

title: Self-Building Labs
authors: Jiaru Bai, Yuchi Zhao, Han Hao, Miroslav Bogdanovic, Yang Cao, Varinia Bernales
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for. Adapting them to a new experiment still takes extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setup given a high-level scientific goal. SBL starts from whatever already exists, from an empty room to a working SDL, and builds the missing capabilities: the lab layout, its digital twin, robot skills, and experimental workflows. We demonstrate the system working across different robots and setups, scaling from a single workstation to laboratories with several robots working together. We validate SBL's end-to-end capabilities through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment. By shifting the role of human researchers from manually configuring and programming device automation to specifying scientific objectives, SBL makes scientific automation more accessible, flexible, and scalable. Project website: https://self-building-labs.github.io/

infographic.key_insight: Self-building laboratories extend automation beyond running experiments to designing, configuring, and operating the laboratory setup itself.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automating lab configuration could reduce manual integration work and make scientific automation more flexible across robots, workstations, and experimental goals.
method: Start from a high-level scientific goal and the available laboratory infrastructure.
Build missing capabilities, including lab layouts, digital twins, robot skills, and experimental workflows.
Coordinate experimental execution across single-workstation and multi-robot setups.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports demonstrations across different robots and setups, including multi-robot laboratories, and end-to-end validation through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify setup effort, reliability, or generalization to experiments beyond the demonstrated configurations.
infographic.paper_title: Self-Building Labs

title: Beyond Large Language Models: A Mental World Model Framework for Mental Modeling, Simulation, Evolution, and Interpretability
authors: Qingshi Wang
abstract: Understanding and simulating how subjective cognition and mental states emerge, evolve, and shape behavior is essential for advancing artificial intelligence toward deeper social cognition and general intelligence. Existing large language models (LLMs) and Theory of Mind (ToM) methods primarily infer mental states from linguistic information, lacking unified mechanisms for subjective world construction, cognitive-psychological interactions, dynamic evolution, and historical dependencies. This paper introduces the Mental World Model (MWM) and its implementation, the Multi-Branch Mental Evolution Architecture (MMEA), which explicitly constructs subjective worlds, models interactions between cognition and mental states, and simulates continuous mental evolution shaped by historical experiences. On DynToM and RecToM, MMEA achieves 96.48% and 94.00% accuracy, respectively, outperforming leading LLMs and specialized ToM methods. Additional experiments demonstrate improvements of 28.7, 39.3, and 16.6 percentage points in mental state and behavior prediction, long-sequence prediction, and implicit mental state inference, respectively. The results demonstrate that MMEA provides an interpretable framework for continuous mental modeling, enabling AI to move beyond surface-level semantic representations to infer individuals' underlying mental states from linguistic information and dynamically simulate their internal cognitive processes and evolution over time. MWM also provides a promising foundation for causal reasoning, personalized AI, sustained human-AI interaction, and future advances toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).

infographic.key_insight: The Mental World Model framework explicitly represents subjective worlds and evolving mental states to support interpretable predictions of cognition and behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its Multi-Branch Mental Evolution Architecture (MMEA) offers a potential approach to history-aware mental-state modeling for personalized AI and sustained human–AI interaction.
method: Construct explicit representations of individuals’ subjective worlds.
Model interactions between cognition and mental states.
Simulate continuous mental evolution shaped by historical experiences.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 96.48% accuracy on DynToM and 94.00% on RecToM, plus gains of 28.7, 39.3, and 16.6 percentage points in mental-state and behavior prediction, long-sequence prediction, and implicit mental-state inference, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark performance does not establish faithful reconstruction of real human mental processes; real-world validity and deployment costs require further evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Large Language Models: A Mental World Model Framework for Mental Modeling, Simulation, Evolution, and Interpretability

title: On the possibilities and limitations of LLM-based multi-agent systems for multi-criteria decision-making in healthcare operations management
authors: Marco Boresta, Tommaso Giovannelli, Sepehr Namirad, Giulia Riccardi
abstract: Multi-criteria models for healthcare operations need weights that express how stakeholders trade off patient waiting time, provider workload, and operating cost, but these weights are difficult to quantify. Teams of large language model (LLM) agents, each prompted to represent a stakeholder, have been used to supply them. We propose a framework for assessing the reliability of LLM-generated preferences as inputs to multi-objective optimization and quantifying how their uncertainty affects decisions. We study explicit preferences by asking agents to rate the importance of the criteria in an outpatient appointment scheduling problem, and implicit preferences by inferring trade-offs from the agents' pairwise choices between emergency department configurations. The computational experiments show that the explicit preferences respond to the clinic's operating conditions and differ across roles, but deliberation among the agents can erase these differences, whereas simple averaging preserves them. The pairwise choices used to reveal the agents' implicit preferences depend largely on which option is presented first, and we find limited evidence that a statistical model using contextual information alongside presentation order predicts the agents' choices on new comparison pairs better than a model using presentation order alone. We then formulate robust weighted-sum optimization models to account for preference uncertainty. In most cases, these models select different schedules or configurations from those obtained using average preference weights. These results indicate that LLM-generated preferences need an audit of this kind before they are used as optimization weights in healthcare decision support.

infographic.key_insight: LLM stakeholder agents can generate healthcare decision weights, but deliberation and presentation-order bias can undermine their reliability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Audit LLM-generated preferences and model their uncertainty before using them as weights in healthcare optimization.
method: Elicit explicit importance ratings for outpatient scheduling criteria from stakeholder-role agents.
Infer implicit trade-offs from pairwise choices between emergency department configurations.
Evaluate preference reliability and compare robust weighted-sum optimization with average-weight solutions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Computational experiments found role- and context-sensitive explicit ratings, strong presentation-order effects in pairwise choices, and robust solutions that differed from average-weight solutions in most cases.
infographic.watch_item: Role-prompted preferences should not be treated as validated stakeholder values; deliberation can erase role differences, and contextual predictors showed limited added predictive value beyond presentation order.
infographic.paper_title: On the possibilities and limitations of LLM-based multi-agent systems for multi-criteria decision-making in healthcare operations management

title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
authors: Rida Assalouh, Tom Jacobs, Rebekka Burkholz, Yani Ioannou, Umut Şimşekli
abstract: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a minorization-maximization surrogate for the exact allocation problem. On ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16, BMuon improves over Muon under gradual structured MLP pruning, and its learned allocations provide a more effective pruning criterion than weight magnitude. On a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves over Muon under post-training MLP channel pruning.

infographic.key_insight: Budget Muon (BMuon) modifies Muon’s spectral geometry so MLP hidden channels compete for a shared budget, making trained Transformers more robust to structured channel pruning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: BMuon offers an interpretable global channel budget and learned pruning scores for reducing Transformer MLP width while preserving more performance than Muon in the reported evaluations.
method: Formulate normalized steepest descent under norms interpolating between Muon’s geometry and structured sparse geometries.
Allocate a shared budget across hidden channels and approximate the exact allocation problem with a minorization–maximization surrogate.
Prove width-minimal minimum-cost representations for linear factorization models under sufficiently scarce BMuon budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improvements over Muon for gradual MLP pruning of ViT-S/16 on ImageNet-1K and post-training MLP pruning of a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb; learned allocations also outperform weight-magnitude pruning scores in the vision evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: The width-minimality guarantee concerns linear factorization models, while practical Transformer training uses an allocation surrogate whose overhead and approximation effects require evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility

title: Quality-of-Transmission Estimation in Quantum Networks: Compute, Simulate, or Learn?
authors: Anis Bekri, Amar Abane, Van Sy Mai, Abdella Battou, Saddek Bensalem
abstract: Future quantum networks will rely on control-plane decisions such as routing, scheduling, entanglement provisioning, purification, and memory allocation. Each decision depends on a timely and reliable estimate of the quality of the entanglement that a candidate path can deliver, with end-to-end fidelity as a central metric. Inspired by the optical-networking experience with quality-of-transmission (QoT) estimation, this article asks when a quantum controller should compute fidelity analytically, simulate it, or learn a surrogate model. The optical analogy is useful but incomplete: optical QoT estimation often predicts a scalar transmission margin, whereas quantum QoT estimation must account for probabilistic entanglement generation, random memory waiting times, decoherence, state consumption, and measurement constraints that can make fidelity a stochastic target. We propose a compute/simulate/learn framework for quantum QoT estimation and illustrate it with a simulation-based proof of concept. Our study shows that analytical composition can be sufficient in simple regimes, that simulation becomes necessary when stochastic memory effects shape the delivered fidelity distribution, and that lightweight learned surrogates can approximate simulator labels at much lower runtime cost for online control. We close with open challenges for deployment, including stochastic targets, sim-to-real transfer, data-generation cost, physics-informed learning, and generalization beyond individual paths to full network topologies.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum-network fidelity estimation should use analytical computation, simulation, or learned surrogates according to the complexity of stochastic effects and online control needs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Timely fidelity estimates can guide routing, scheduling, entanglement provisioning, purification, and quantum-memory allocation.
method: Compute fidelity analytically in simple regimes.
Simulate probabilistic entanglement generation, memory waiting times, and decoherence.
Train lightweight surrogates to approximate simulator outputs for online control.
infographic.evidence_signal: A simulation-based proof of concept shows that stochastic memory effects can require distribution-level fidelity estimates, while learned surrogates approximate simulator labels at much lower runtime cost.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment requires validation beyond simulator-generated labels, particularly for sim-to-real transfer and generalization to full network topologies.
infographic.paper_title: Quality-of-Transmission Estimation in Quantum Networks: Compute, Simulate, or Learn?

title: Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere
authors: Joshua Williamson, Niall Jeffrey, Lorne Whiteway
abstract: Many of the most important datasets in the physical sciences live natively on the sphere, and these data often carry no preferred position or orientation. Using methods that do not reflect this symmetry leads to far higher simulation requirements, which can be catastrophic for scientific analyses (forcing reliance on cheap, imperfect models that bias results). We present a novel spherical implementation of a gauge equivariant mesh architecture that is specifically designed for the Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (\healpix{}) of the sphere. The $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-equivariant convolution is built from steerable filters, parallel transport and spin-weighted features. The architecture supplies the exact symmetry, so the network does not spend training data learning it. The convolution operations are constructed to give provably exact equivariance, given a band-limit. Our full CNNs can achieve SO(3)-invariance error at per-cent-level and lower, which is controlled through well-understood hyperparameters. On benchmarks, our technique gives the most accurate dense gradient regression and competitive cosmic microwave background foreground removal and denoising. The improved simulation efficiency matters most in simulation-based inference (SBI), where high-fidelity simulations are expensive and neural compressors require large training sets, so a fixed budget forces analyses with less accurate simulators. In cosmology lensing SBI, our technique yields the tightest posteriors at matched simulation count. This approach is a novel method that will enable new convolutional neural network analyses, including generative and inference tasks, for processes and data on the sphere.

infographic.key_insight: Building rotational symmetry into spherical CNNs reduces the need to learn it from data, improving simulation efficiency for scientific inference.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture supports learning on HEALPix spherical data when expensive simulations and arbitrary orientations make conventional CNN training inefficient.
method: Adapt a gauge-equivariant mesh architecture to the HEALPix sphere.
Combine steerable filters, parallel transport and spin-weighted features.
Construct convolutions with provably exact SO(3) equivariance under a band-limit assumption.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports the most accurate dense gradient regression, competitive CMB foreground removal and denoising, and the tightest cosmological lensing posteriors at matched simulation counts.
infographic.watch_item: Exact equivariance applies to band-limited convolutions; full-network invariance remains approximate, with reported errors at percent level or lower depending on hyperparameters.
infographic.paper_title: Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere

title: DrugHarness: An Evolvable Agent Harness for Computational Drug Discovery
authors: Yuxing Chen, Zhisheng Zhang, Cheng Tang, Wei Li, Minghui Zhang, Ziyan Huang
abstract: Computational drug discovery requires agents to compose scientific operations and adapt to changing evidence and constraints. Here we introduce DrugHarness, an evolvable agent harness coupling composable scientific execution with conditional skill induction. Its environment integrates over 80 scientific operations, biomedical resources and task-specific code, preserving associations among candidates, results and artifacts. From execution trajectories and outcome feedback, DrugHarness induces action hypotheses with observable applicability conditions, recommended actions and supporting evidence. An independent review agent evaluates candidate skills derived from these hypotheses through source verification and, when needed, targeted execution trials. Admitted skills guide subsequent tasks and are revised through feedback. Evaluation on MolBench and SMDD-Bench demonstrates capabilities in molecular screening, optimization and constrained design. Without evolution, DrugHarness exceeds reported MolClaw-CC results by 10.8 percentage points in affinity-comparison accuracy and 55% in mean top-three active hits on MolBench. Retrospective evaluation on skill-development tasks shows that evolution increases Qwen's affinity-comparison accuracy from 62.2% to 81.1% and optimization success from 79.5% to 87.2%. In a prospective HPK1 study, DrugHarness achieves a more favorable median docking score than Biomni among system-specific candidates. A synthesized compound achieves a cellular IC50 of 14.19 nM, a 2.64-fold potency improvement over the best input reference, with activity competitive with two selected compounds designed by experienced medicinal chemists. These results support conditional skill evolution for scientific agents and demonstrate a workflow connecting computational drug design with experimental validation.

infographic.key_insight: DrugHarness turns execution feedback into reviewed, condition-specific skills that guide later computational drug-discovery tasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The harness combines composable scientific tools, linked experimental artifacts and evidence-checked skill updates to support adaptable discovery workflows.
method: Integrate over 80 scientific operations with biomedical resources and task-specific code.
Induce candidate skills with observable applicability conditions, recommended actions and supporting evidence.
Use an independent agent to verify sources and, when needed, run targeted trials before admitting skills.
infographic.evidence_signal: On retrospective skill-development tasks, evolution raised Qwen’s affinity-comparison accuracy from 62.2% to 81.1%; in a prospective HPK1 study, a synthesized compound achieved cellular IC50 of 14.19 nM, a 2.64-fold potency improvement over the best input reference.
infographic.watch_item: Retrospective skill-development gains and one prospective HPK1 study do not establish generalization across unseen targets or discovery settings.
infographic.paper_title: DrugHarness: An Evolvable Agent Harness for Computational Drug Discovery

title: Active Learning for Interatomic Potentials: A Review of Uncertainty-Driven Data Efficiency
authors: Ilya V. Chepkasov, Alexander V. Shapeev, Alexander G. Kvashnin
abstract: Developing a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) that is accurate for the specific conditions under which it will be applied, rather than simply for the predefined configurations chosen by the model developer, is a significant challenge in atomistic simulation. Active learning (AL) addresses this challenge by closing the loop between candidate generation, data selection, reference calculation, and model updating. Here, we survey more than seventy studies, with an emphasis on work from 2020 to 2026, to understand how active learning has evolved from a niche, on-the-fly training technique for query-by-committee and Gaussian process force fields into a diverse family of data-efficient strategies. he reviewed examples include on-the-fly molecular dynamics, active data selection for fine-tuning pretrained models, kernel- and representation-based acquisition using frozen pretrained models, and reaction-aware sampling for chemical systems far from equilibrium. We explore the use of active learning in elemental and alloy mechanics, hydrogen and ion diffusion, ferroelectrics and effective Hamiltonians of functional materials, reactive and photochemical dynamics, high-entropy and compositionally disordered materials, as well as generative and autonomous material discovery pipelines. Drawing on a growing body of critical, methodologically self-aware literature, we also show that this achievement carries systematic caveats. Uncertainty estimates are not interchangeable across model architectures and are frequently the least reliable exactly where they matter most. We close by discussing the outlook for standardized, uncertainty-calibrated, and observable-targeted active-learning workflows in the foundation-model era.

infographic.key_insight: Active learning makes interatomic-potential training more data-efficient by selecting new reference calculations for the conditions where a model will be used.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Uncertainty-driven sampling can focus expensive reference calculations on configurations relevant to mechanics, diffusion, functional materials, and reactive dynamics.
method: Generate candidate atomic configurations and select informative samples.
Run reference calculations, update the potential, and repeat.
Use committee, Gaussian-process, pretrained-representation, or reaction-aware acquisition strategies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The review surveys more than 70 studies, emphasizing 2020–2026, but the abstract reports no pooled quantitative efficiency or accuracy benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: Uncertainty estimates are architecture-dependent and may be least reliable in unfamiliar regimes where dependable selection matters most.
infographic.paper_title: Active Learning for Interatomic Potentials: A Review of Uncertainty-Driven Data Efficiency

title: AI-Driven Reproducibility and Analytical Robustness in Scientific Discovery
authors: Shicheng Liu, Krista Opsahl-Ong, Andrew Drozdov, Julian Killingback, Arnav Singhvi, Ronak Pradeep
abstract: Reproducible and analytically robust research findings are essential to scientific progress, but evaluating these properties typically requires costly manual effort. We investigate whether LLM agents can help automate reproduction and robustness analysis, using a medical case study grounded in the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, a widely used U.S. cancer registry underlying tens of thousands of published studies. First, we introduce SEER-Repro, a benchmark of 20 published SEER-based papers together with the data and resources required to reproduce their findings. Second, we create an AI agent that successfully reproduces 77.4% of 2,190 atomic claims, while providing executable baselines for further analysis. Third, we develop an agentic analysis pipeline to test the robustness of the medical findings by identifying analytical choices underlying each finding, proposing defensible alternatives, and rerunning the analysis to determine whether those choices affect the conclusion. Across published papers in SEER-Repro, our pipeline identifies potentially consequential analytical choices in 9.5% of fully reproduced findings and flags them for expert review. These results show how LLM agents can support scientific review by reproducing findings, systematically testing their robustness, and directing expert attention toward potentially consequential analytical choices.

infographic.key_insight: LLM agents can help reproduce published findings and identify analytical choices that warrant expert review.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Executable reproduction baselines paired with automated robustness checks offer a practical workflow for auditing data-driven research.
method: Build SEER-Repro from 20 published cancer-registry studies and their reproduction resources.
Use an AI agent to reproduce atomic claims and generate executable analysis baselines.
Identify analytical choices, test defensible alternatives, and flag potentially consequential changes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The agent reproduced 77.4% of 2,190 atomic claims; the robustness pipeline flagged potentially consequential analytical choices in 9.5% of fully reproduced findings.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from one medical-registry benchmark, and flagged analytical choices require expert review rather than establishing that a finding is invalid.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Driven Reproducibility and Analytical Robustness in Scientific Discovery

title: GLOBE: Evolving Structured Agentic Memory for E-commerce Product Optimization in Generative Search
authors: Hyunseo Kim, Suil Choe, Sukkyoung So, Daeyeon Yi
abstract: Optimizing product listings for generative search requires language agents not only to rewrite effectively but also to continually self-improve by retaining successful strategies across diverse categories. However, existing approaches often treat structured listings as free-form text, leaving effective strategies implicit in prompts, search trajectories, or rewritten outputs rather than accumulating them as a reusable agentic memory. To address this limitation, we introduce GLOBE, an agentic framework that drives continual self-improvement by storing optimization knowledge in an evolving handbook of explicit, field-scoped behaviors. In each episode, an Editor applies relevant behaviors and receives rank-based feedback, which a Reflector converts into behavior updates. Crucially for dependable execution in real-world settings, a Moderator removes redundant proposals, a Curator commits accepted changes, and consistently harmful behaviors are deactivated. This cycle transforms episodic feedback into a persistent, field-scoped optimization memory. Experiments show that structured behaviors outperform monolithic prompt optimization, while feedback-driven evolution and moderation further improve effectiveness and reduce downside risk. The learned behaviors also remain effective on unseen product categories, suggesting that agentic memory evolution supports interpretable and transferable product optimization.

infographic.key_insight: GLOBE turns rank-based feedback into an evolving handbook of explicit, field-scoped behaviors for optimizing product listings in generative search.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reusable optimization memory offers a more inspectable alternative to monolithic prompts, with moderation and deactivation mechanisms to limit harmful updates.
method: An Editor applies relevant handbook behaviors to product listing fields.
A Reflector converts rank-based feedback into proposed behavior updates.
A Moderator removes redundant proposals, a Curator commits accepted changes, and consistently harmful behaviors are deactivated.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports gains over monolithic prompt optimization, further improvements from feedback-driven evolution and moderation, and transfer to unseen product categories, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment should verify that rank-based feedback reliably reflects optimization quality before committing persistent behavior updates.
infographic.paper_title: GLOBE: Evolving Structured Agentic Memory for E-commerce Product Optimization in Generative Search

title: Deep LLM layers expose passage-level context in EEG during silent reading
authors: Ingo Marquardt, Anthilia Alchanat, Priyanka Jain
abstract: In a previous report we showed that a decoder can recover open-vocabulary word-level information from 19-channel EEG recorded during silent reading, by aligning short EEG windows with hidden-state embeddings of the presented word taken from a large language model (LLM). That analysis contrasted two of the model's 33 layers: the context-free input embedding and one mid-depth layer. Here we ask how EEG-decodable structure is distributed over the full depth of the language model. We trained one decoder per layer of Llama-3.1-8B, with and without a causal transformer over the sequence of EEG windows. We distinguish word-level decodability from a context-tracking component. Word-level decodability peaks in early layers and declines steadily towards the last layer. In contrast, the context-tracking component of the retrieval gain rises with depth, both with and without a causal transformer. Unexpectedly, a decoder that sees a single 0.5-s window at a time tracks the text passage too. Two new controls dissect this component. A target-geometry control, a synthetic predictor made of the true target plus noise calibrated to each decoder's word-level accuracy, shows that context tracking is not a by-product of word decoding and target geometry. A control that permutes predictions across runs from either the same or from different sessions shows that most of the observed context-tracking is not caused by an EEG recording session signature. Instead, context tracking mostly follows the text. A single EEG window therefore carries passage-level information that a contextual target can absorb. The results locate word identity in the early layers of the language model, discourse state in the deeper layers, and make the choice of target layer a design dial for EEG language decoders.

infographic.key_insight: EEG decoding favors word identity in early LLM layers and passage-level context in deeper layers, even from a single 0.5-second EEG window.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Target-layer selection offers a design dial for EEG language decoders, trading word-level decodability against passage-context tracking.
method: Train a separate EEG-to-embedding decoder for each Llama-3.1-8B layer.
Compare decoding with and without a causal transformer over EEG-window sequences.
Test context tracking using accuracy-calibrated synthetic predictors and within- versus across-session prediction permutations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 19-channel EEG during silent reading, word-level decodability peaked early and declined with layer depth, while context tracking increased; controls indicated it mostly followed the text rather than recording-session signatures.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report sample size or effect sizes, limiting assessment of robustness and generalizability.
infographic.paper_title: Deep LLM layers expose passage-level context in EEG during silent reading

title: RL-Guided Temporal Localization for Dual-Channel Retrieval in Long-Horizon Agent Memory
authors: Dabin Sheng, Zhe Wu, Jinming Zhao, Junliang Xing, Yuanchun Shi
abstract: Time-aware retrieval is crucial for long-horizon LLM agents to effectively leverage ever-growing long-term memory. Existing methods focus on lexical or semantic similarity, leading to target memories being crowded out by temporally mismatched yet semantically similar candidates. Even time-aware approaches inject temporal cues only during memory organization or answer generation, overlooking temporal constraints at the retrieval stage, where candidate selection occurs - the root cause of the displacement. Inspired by the temporal contiguity effect in human episodic memory, we propose TIDER (Temporal Interval-driven Dual-channel Evidence Retrieval), a time-aware agentic retrieval framework. Central to TIDER is a reinforcement learning (RL)-trained temporal interval locator that infers the temporal windows in which the evidence lies. RL optimizes window localization as a discrete, non-differentiable retrieval decision, using composite rewards to convert sparse answer supervision into fine-grained retrieval feedback. These temporal windows first define the temporal retrieval channel; the retrieved candidates are then merged with results from the semantic channel and reranked by proximity to the windows. This temporal grounding enables TIDER to retrieve temporally aligned evidence that would otherwise be drowned out by the volume of semantically similar yet temporally mismatched memories. With a lightweight 1.7B locator, TIDER achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on both long-horizon memory benchmarks - 61.52% on LifeBench (+8.82%) and 78.96% on LoCoMo (+3.66%) - which indicates that temporal cues are crucial for pinpointing target evidence amid a vast pool of semantically similar historical events in long-term daily-life memory.

infographic.key_insight: TIDER improves long-term agent memory retrieval by locating relevant time windows so temporally mismatched but semantically similar memories do not crowd out target evidence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Memory systems for long-horizon LLM agents can combine temporal and semantic retrieval to better distinguish similar events occurring at different times.
method: Train a lightweight 1.7B temporal interval locator with reinforcement learning and composite rewards derived from answer supervision.
Retrieve candidates through separate temporal-window and semantic channels.
Merge candidates and rerank them by proximity to the predicted time windows.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art accuracy of 61.52% on LifeBench (+8.82%) and 78.96% on LoCoMo (+3.66%).
infographic.watch_item: Incorrectly localized time windows could weaken retrieval; the abstract does not report robustness to ambiguous temporal cues or inference overhead.
infographic.paper_title: RL-Guided Temporal Localization for Dual-Channel Retrieval in Long-Horizon Agent Memory

title: From Trajectories to Differentiated Skills: Cognitive Differentiation for Self-Improving Agents
authors: Yewei Zhao, Derong Xu, Wei Chen, Yin Xu, Peilun Zhou, Xiaohan Wang
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents tackle complex tasks through reasoning and interaction with external environments. Agent skills provide persistent, transferable capabilities that guide task planning, inform contextual decisions, support tool use, and enable executable procedures. Yet existing skill-evolution methods largely organize knowledge around skill artifacts, overlooking the functional heterogeneity within individual skills and its implications for knowledge maintenance and use. Inspired by cognitive science, we propose Cognitive Differentiation in Skill Evolution (CDSE), which evolves a unified skill through four functionally distinct yet coordinated components: Meta, Experience, Tool, and Script. CDSE extracts evidence-grounded semantic gradients from successful and failed trajectories, consolidates them by functional role, and applies component-specific updates and validation with cross-component coordination and adaptive invocation. An analysis of 500 top-ranked skill packages shows that 96.8% contain knowledge spanning at least two functional roles. Across six benchmarks, three agent models, and two execution harnesses, CDSE achieves the highest scores in all 36 settings, improving over the Base agent by 7.6 percentage points and the strongest competing method in each setting by 2.6 points on average. Ablation studies further support the importance of functional differentiation and adaptive invocation.

infographic.key_insight: CDSE improves self-evolving LLM agents by differentiating each skill into four coordinated functional components: Meta, Experience, Tool, and Script.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Role-specific skill updates and adaptive invocation offer a structured way to maintain reusable agent knowledge across planning, decisions, tool use, and execution.
method: Extract evidence-grounded semantic gradients from successful and failed trajectories.
Consolidate learning by functional role and apply component-specific updates and validation.
Coordinate components and adaptively invoke relevant skill knowledge.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six benchmarks, three agent models, and two execution harnesses, CDSE led all 36 settings, averaging gains of 7.6 percentage points over Base and 2.6 points over the strongest competitor in each setting.
infographic.watch_item: Component-specific validation and cross-component coordination add implementation complexity; their operational overhead is not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: From Trajectories to Differentiated Skills: Cognitive Differentiation for Self-Improving Agents

title: Beyond SAEs: Consistent Concept Discovery with Sparse Coding
authors: Jinho Choi, Hyesu Lim, Jaegul Choo, Steffen Schneider
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) explain foundation model representations by decomposing activations into sparse combinations of learned dictionary atoms. However, the learned dictionaries can vary across training runs, limiting the reliability and reproducibility of SAE-based analyses. We propose Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL), which replaces the standard linear encoder with per-sample sparse coding. This is motivated by our synthetic analysis showing that coefficients from a single linear encoder pass are suboptimal compared with those obtained by per-sample optimization, suggesting that sparse coding is a reliable mechanism for dictionary learning. Across 16 synthetic settings, ConSDL achieves near-perfect dictionary and coefficient recovery. These gains translate to state-of-the-art cross-seed consistency across four vision and language settings, where ConSDL improves dictionary and coefficient consistency by 17.6% and 35.9%, respectively, over the average of six SAE baselines.

infographic.key_insight: ConSDL discovers more reproducible concepts by replacing a sparse autoencoder’s single-pass linear encoder with per-sample sparse coding.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More consistent dictionaries and coefficients across training seeds can make foundation-model interpretability analyses more reliable.
method: Optimize sparse coefficients separately for each sample instead of using a single linear encoder pass.
Learn dictionaries through Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL).
Evaluate dictionary and coefficient recovery and cross-seed consistency.
infographic.evidence_signal: ConSDL achieves near-perfect recovery across 16 synthetic settings and, across four vision and language settings, improves dictionary and coefficient consistency by 17.6% and 35.9% over the average of six SAE baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Per-sample optimization may add computational cost; the abstract does not report runtime or scaling trade-offs.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond SAEs: Consistent Concept Discovery with Sparse Coding

title: SkillBrowser: Selective Skill Exposure for Scalable Skill-Using Agents
authors: Jin Ye, Yifan Jiang, Lan-zhe Guo
abstract: Large language model agents increasingly rely on skills to extend their capabilities in complex tasks. However, scalable skill use requires Selective Skill Exposure (SSE): providing relevant procedural content when needed while avoiding unnecessary exposure that may disrupt reasoning. Existing paradigms fall short in complementary ways. Progressive disclosure exposes metadata for a growing skill library, introducing context pollution; retrieval limits catalog exposure, but static retrieval from the initial task query may be misaligned with capability needs that emerge during reasoning and may still inject unnecessary skills. We propose SkillBrowser, a Meta-Skill-managed framework that enables an agent to identify current capability needs, formulate targeted queries, and selectively load skills on demand. Across six SRA-Bench subsets and five LLMs, SkillBrowser improves aggregate accuracy over static retrieval and LLM-based selection, including multi-step tool use, and mitigates accuracy degradation on already-solvable instances. Benefits remain model- and task-dependent, with under-invocation of useful skills and additional latency as key limitations. These results demonstrate the viability of Meta-Skill-managed SSE for scalable skill repositories.

infographic.key_insight: SkillBrowser lets agents selectively load skills as capability needs emerge, improving accuracy while limiting unnecessary context exposure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: On-demand skill loading offers a practical way to scale agent skill repositories without exposing the full catalog or relying solely on initial-query retrieval.
method: Use a Meta-Skill to identify current capability needs during reasoning.
Formulate targeted queries for relevant skills.
Load procedural content selectively when needed.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six SRA-Bench subsets and five LLMs, SkillBrowser improves aggregate accuracy over static retrieval and LLM-based selection, including multi-step tool use, and reduces degradation on already-solvable instances.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits vary by model and task; agents may under-invoke useful skills, and the framework adds latency.
infographic.paper_title: SkillBrowser: Selective Skill Exposure for Scalable Skill-Using Agents

title: Reason-guided Human Reward Modeling for Preference-based Reinforcement Learning
authors: Anshul Nayak, Shahil Shaik, Jonathan Smereka, Yue Wang
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies optimized for task rewards may produce behaviors that are efficient but misaligned with human expectations, safety preferences, or intent. This paper presents a reason-guided preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) framework that learns a human reward model from trajectory-level feedback. In addition to preference labels, the framework incorporates reason tags explaining why a behavior is preferred, enabling the learned reward to capture both human choices and their underlying rationale. Compared with preference-only reward learning, the reason-guided formulation provides additional supervision for learning human-aligned rewards and improves the interpretability of the resulting policy. The learned human reward is combined with the environment reward during policy optimization, allowing the agent to improve task performance while producing more interpretable, human- aligned, and preference-sensitive behavior

infographic.key_insight: Adding reason tags to trajectory preferences helps an RL reward model capture both human choices and their underlying rationale.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining learned human rewards with environment rewards can support task-effective agent behavior that better reflects human expectations and safety preferences.
method: Collect trajectory-level preference labels and reason tags.
Learn a human reward model using both feedback types.
Optimize the policy with combined human and environment rewards.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved interpretability versus preference-only reward learning but provides no datasets, benchmarks, or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation must balance human and environment rewards, and reason-tag collection adds annotation requirements.
infographic.paper_title: Reason-guided Human Reward Modeling for Preference-based Reinforcement Learning

title: Scalable long-range machine learning interatomic potentials with electrical response for atomistic material modeling
authors: Yicheng Chen, Xiaoyun Yu, Hyejeong Song, Xintian Wang, Zihui Li, Zixi Xia
abstract: Accurate atomistic simulations of materials under electric fields require long-range electrostatics and electrical-response modeling at length scales beyond the reach of conventional first-principles methods. Yet these capabilities remain difficult to reconcile with the scalability of machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs). Strictly local models enable efficient spatial parallelization but neglect long-range interactions, whereas existing electrostatic extensions introduce global dependencies that hinder distributed computation. Here, we overcome this limitation by analytically separating the long-range electrostatic forces and Born effective charges (BECs) into a global electrostatics calculation and strictly local derivatives of learned latent charges. This formulation preserves the spatial decomposability of equivariant MLIPs while enabling distributed evaluation of energies, forces, stresses, and BECs across different boundary conditions. Implemented as DPA4C-LR on the \texttt{nvalchemi} platform, the framework scales to 5.2 million atoms on four GPUs at approximately twice the computational cost of its short-range backbone. Trained on energies and forces, DPA4C-LR accurately infers BECs and reproduces the field-dependent infrared spectra of water. We further demonstrate its capabilities by recovering the characteristic slim polarization hysteresis of relaxor \ce{Pb(Mg_{1/3}Nb_{2/3})O3}, which is obscured by finite-size effects in smaller simulations; predicting a room-temperature field-driven ionic conductivity of $6.8 \pm 0.7$~mS/cm in amorphous \ce{Li_{0.9}NbO_{0.9}Cl_{4.1}}; and modeling interfacial thermal transport across Si/diamond interfaces with slab-corrected electrostatics. By combining long-range physics, electrical-response inference, and distributed computation, this framework extends predictive atomistic modeling toward device-relevant length scales.

infographic.key_insight: DPA4C-LR combines long-range electrostatics and electrical-response prediction with spatially decomposable machine-learning interatomic potentials.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables large-scale atomistic modeling of field-dependent material behavior and interfacial thermal transport toward device-relevant length scales.
method: Separate electrostatic forces and Born effective charges into global electrostatics and strictly local derivatives of learned latent charges.
Preserve spatial decomposition for distributed evaluation of energies, forces, stresses, and electrical response.
Implement DPA4C-LR on nvalchemi with support for different electrostatic boundary conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports scaling to 5.2 million atoms on four GPUs at approximately twice the short-range backbone cost, plus demonstrations spanning water infrared spectra, relaxor hysteresis, ionic conductivity, and Si/diamond thermal transport.
infographic.watch_item: Global electrostatics and boundary-condition handling remain implementation concerns; the abstract does not establish scaling efficiency beyond four GPUs.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable long-range machine learning interatomic potentials with electrical response for atomistic material modeling

title: Deconstructing Multi-Task Active Learning: The Paradox of Gradient Conflict and Orthogonal Decomposition
authors: Juho Jung, Seongjae Kang, Jinyoung Han
abstract: Existing multi-task active learning (MTL-AL) methods predominantly rely on linear scalarization of heterogeneous objectives such as uncertainty, diversity, and gradient conflict. We argue that this entangled formulation is fundamentally limited, as linear combination fails to capture Pareto-optimal trade-offs under conflicting objectives. We propose a shift from combination to deconstruction and introduce a principled framework that rethinks MTL-AL along three orthogonal dimensions. First, we identify the Conflict Paradox: although the optimization literature treats gradient conflict as interference to be suppressed, penalizing conflict when ranking candidates is measurably worse than not scoring it at all. We therefore decouple the two concerns: the acquisition function does not score conflict, and the resulting interference is resolved by gradient surgery during training. Second, we introduce Orthogonal Decomposition, separating acquisition into Informativeness and Exploration. This two-stage process, informativeness filtering followed by coverage maximization, prevents "diversity dilution" by excluding uninformative outliers before enforcing diversity. Third, we propose Cross-Task Mutual Information (CTMI), a covariance-based statistic of cross-task dependency computed from MC-dropout task entropies. Extensive experiments on COCO, Cityscapes, and NYUv2, including comparisons against recent MTL-AL and data-selection baselines, demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, highlighting that structural rethinking of acquisition yields larger gains than incremental heuristic design. Code is available at https://github.com/Juho-Jung/multitask_active_learning_official.

infographic.key_insight: Multi-task active learning benefits from separating informativeness, exploration, and training-time gradient conflict resolution rather than combining them into one acquisition score.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a way to select informative, diverse samples for multi-task models while handling gradient interference during training.
method: Exclude gradient conflict from acquisition scoring; address it through gradient surgery during training.
Filter candidates by informativeness, then maximize coverage to avoid selecting uninformative outliers.
Estimate cross-task dependency with Cross-Task Mutual Information, a covariance-based statistic computed from MC-dropout task entropies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent improvements over recent multi-task active learning and data-selection baselines on COCO, Cityscapes, and NYUv2, but provides no numerical gains.
infographic.watch_item: MC-dropout sampling and gradient surgery introduce computational costs that should be measured against annotation savings.
infographic.paper_title: Deconstructing Multi-Task Active Learning: The Paradox of Gradient Conflict and Orthogonal Decomposition
